vignette:
He is 46, an African man who has spent most of his adult life outdoors. Now he works as a park ranger, and people who meet him at the trailhead often see someone steady and capable: a man who knows animal tracks, can read weather from the sky, and speaks calmly to tourists when they wander too close to dangerous ground. It is only after several conversations that the shape of his life begins to emerge, and how much of it is still organized around a war that officially ended years ago.

He grows up in a rural area where the boundary between ordinary life and political violence gradually disappears. As a young man, he joins a military force during a period of armed conflict. At first he describes it as something he does because other young men are doing it, because there is pressure, because there are few real choices. He learns to move on little sleep, to stay alert to sound, to notice the difference between wind in the grass and footsteps. He also learns how quickly a familiar face can become a body.

The event he returns to most often happens during a patrol. His unit is moving through scrubland in the early morning when gunfire breaks out from a place that had seemed empty. He remembers dropping to the ground and the smell of dust kicked into his mouth. He remembers shouting that does not sound human to him now, and the confusion of trying to locate where the shots are coming from. A man beside him, someone he has eaten with and joked with the night before, is hit. He sees the wound, sees the shock on his friend’s face, and then sees more gunfire coming toward them. He cannot reach him without exposing himself. He stays where he is. Later, after the attack ends, the friend is dead. He says that from that moment onward, something in him becomes divided: the part that keeps moving and following orders, and the part that remains fixed there in the dust, beside a man he believes he abandoned.

He survives the rest of the conflict by becoming emotionally narrow and practical. He does what is needed, keeps his weapon clean, scans every tree line, sleeps lightly. When the war ends and he returns to civilian life, those habits do not fade. At first people praise him for being disciplined. He marries, finds work, and eventually becomes a park ranger, a job that suits his love of land and his ability to stay calm in isolated places. Yet the same skills that make him good at his work are tangled with the war. He walks patrol routes with his shoulders tight, automatically checking high ground and listening for sudden cracks in the bush. If a vehicle backfires near the park entrance, his body reacts before his mind does; he turns sharply, heart pounding, eyes searching for cover. He feels ashamed each time this happens, especially if junior staff are nearby.

At night he rarely rests fully. He wakes drenched in sweat after dreams that place him back in that ambush. In the dream, his friend is sometimes calling his name. Other times he is the one who is injured, unable to move while others leave him behind. His wife tells him that he kicks in his sleep and sometimes shouts in a voice she does not recognize. On those nights he gets out of bed and walks outside, checking locks, scanning darkness he knows is only his own yard. He does not want to explain any of this to her, because he worries she already carries too much of his silence.

During the day he tries not to think about the war, but avoidance takes a great deal of effort. He changes the radio station if news of conflict comes on. He does not attend public ceremonies for veterans. When former fighters gather and retell stories, he keeps away, telling others he is busy with work in the park. He has never returned to the area where he fought. He says it is better not to open graves in the mind, but the memories surface anyway—when he smells smoke, when he hears helicopters overhead, when he sees a young ranger laughing with a colleague and suddenly remembers the friend who died.

His marriage has endured, though not without strain. His wife experiences him as physically present but often far away. He is protective of his family to a degree that sometimes feels excessive even to him. He insists on knowing where his children are, worries if they are late, checks doors multiple times before bed. Crowded markets exhaust him; he positions himself near exits and studies strangers’ hands without meaning to. He startles easily and then grows irritable, embarrassed by how quickly anger rises in him. He says he no longer likes the man he becomes when he feels cornered.

What troubles him most is not only fear but guilt. He speaks of his dead friend as if the man remains in conversation with him. In quiet moments at work, standing watch over a landscape that should be peaceful, he finds himself wondering why he is the one who gets to grow older, to have a wife, to know the names of birds and seasons, while another man’s life ended in the dirt. He understands, rationally, that he was trying to survive. But in his body and in the private court of his mind, the case has never been settled.
